Three years ago, Israel was the victim of a terrorist attack by Hamas that killed nearly 1,200 civilians. Innocent lives were snuffed out, families murdered in cold blood, women raped, young people targeted because of who they are and where they called home.

But the violence of that day did not end on October 8. Its violence was contagious, plunging the region into chaos and years of war that have taken a toll on many thousands of people — Palestinians and Israelis. Israeli civilians were held hostage in dark tunnels by Hamas for hundreds of days, while being subject to rape, torture and murder. Palestinian civilians lost their lives as whole neighborhoods were destroyed, and they continue to endure, unimaginable conditions in Gaza; Palestinians still suffer increased violence and displacement in the West Bank. Civilians in Israel still live in fear of another promised attack by Hamas terrorists, and civilians in Northern Israel or Lebanon worry about being collateral damage in the continuing struggle between Israel and Hezbollah.

After three years, the pathway to peace and a lasting two-state solution is farther out of reach and tattered, while extremist voices have flourished in the Middle East.

This anniversary should be a solemn moment to recommit to the goal of two sovereign states, and rebuilding the pathway to that future. Just as we pushed to bring hostages home and achieve a ceasefire, we must continue to push for expanded aid to rebuild Gaza, for an end to Hamas’ ability to threaten Israel, and for a lasting agreement to end this conflict and ensure that Israelis and Palestinians may live side by side in peace, security, dignity, and mutual recognition.

Three years ago today, Hamas terrorists launched a brutal, barbaric — most inhumane — attack on the people of Israel. Homes, Kibbutzim, and families were burned. Families torn apart. Unspeakable crimes committed against women, children, and seniors. More than 1,200 people were killed and 250 taken hostage, including American citizens.

The cruelty and brutality of this attack demanded universal, international condemnation and American support for our ally and friend Israel.

I have traveled to Israel several times since October 7th, to meet with grieving Israeli families and government leaders. I met twice with Prime Minister Netanyahu, urging him to pursue justice — a just war — not vengeance, to be a partner for peace.

Today, thanks to the tireless advocacy from the families and to American leadership, all the living hostages have been reunited with their loved ones. The dead have been returned to be buried with dignity. Around the world, Jewish people just celebrated their first Rosh Hashanah without any hostages held in Hamas’ custody. But the scars of October 7th run deep and are lasting. The families of those who were killed, and those who were taken, will carry that grief for the rest of their lives. We all will.

Meanwhile, the region remains in turmoil. Millions of Gazans are still displaced and vulnerable, struggling to find the food, water, medicine, and shelter they need to survive. More than 70,000 innocent Palestinian civilians have been killed and thousands more wounded, so many of them children. and Israeli violations of the ceasefire are alarmingly common. In the West Bank, Israeli settlers continue to encroach on Palestinian land, using violence to injure, kill, and drive out Palestinian families, jeopardizing any chance at peace.

We owe it to all those who died, on that day and in the devastating war since, to build a better future.

In this work, I am guided by the Jewish teaching of “Tikkun Olam”— the call to repair the world — and by the Scripture which tells us: blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called children of God.

Today, we remember the suffering of October 7th. Tomorrow, we must continue the work, with mercy and moral clarity, each doing our part to make peace.

Today marks three painful years past the October 7th terrorist attack on Israel, when Hamas murdered more than 1,200 men, women, and children and abducted 251 others into brutal captivity. My heart and thoughts are with the countless families who have suffered an unthinkable, unbearable grief that came with that terrible day and will stay with them forever.

The vile tide of antisemitism and islamophobia that arrived in the October 7th attack’s aftermath has been felt by innocents throughout our world, including far too many of our Jewish and Muslim neighbors across Brooklyn. In the name of all those we have lost, and all others we hope to save, we must continue to stand against hatred in all its forms. The work of building a future where our coexistence is accepted as a source of strength, and not seen as an excuse to divide, must go on.

We can create a world where all are welcome, and safe, and loved – but only if we try.

Over the past week, I have been rewatching gut-wrenching videos taken by Hamas terrorists of their own massacre of Israeli families, grandparents and children three years ago today, reading about new accounts of hostages in brutal captivity, and thinking back to my own experience taking my young children back and forth to a bomb shelter as rockets rained down from Gaza. I think often about how the Iron Dome may very well have saved my family’s lives that day, along with thousands of other innocent civilians in Israel. 

Since 2007 when Israel withdrew from Gaza and turned control over to Hamas, neither Israel nor Gazan civilians have been in charge. Instead, it has been governed by a globally-designated terrorist group whose stated mission and sole focus is to wipe out Israel, which they tried to do three years ago and then carried on for years by holding hundreds of Israeli hostages in brutal conditions in their terror tunnel network. That terrorist group remains armed and dangerous in Gaza today, still fully committed to wiping out Israel, the world’s only safe haven for Jews and the only democracy in the region. 

If you are someone — like me — who wants peace in the region and self-determination for all people there, then Hamas represents a complete and total obstacle to that goal. As we remember the devastation inflicted by them on this day three years ago, we must also recognize that Iranian-backed terrorist groups such as Hamas remain an existential threat not only to peace in the region but also to democracy around the world. 

Today is a day of mourning and remembrance of all those innocent lives lost, those who were wounded both physically and mentally, the hostages who survived through unspeakable conditions, and a country shaken to its core by the genocidal attack three years ago. Tomorrow, I will continue working towards a path to peace, security and self-determination for Israelis and Palestinians alike.

Am Yisrael Chai.
